guideTitle: Best Deep Fryers With Oil Filtration (2026)
metaTitle: Best Deep Fryers With Oil Filtration (2026)
metaDescription: Six deep fryers with oil filtration or drain systems compared by how they filter and store oil, capacity, wattage, dishwasher-safe parts and cleanup effort.
expertTake: The All-Clad 3.5 liter is the pick for a premium home fryer with patented filtration and dishwasher-safe parts, and the T-fal 3.5 liter is the proven value pick. The VEVOR 9.51 quart is the pick for a bar or a big family that needs a faucet drain. If you fry only a few times a year, a manual strainer and a funnel are enough.
introParagraphs: Oil is the hidden cost of frying, and filtration is how a fryer reduces it. A machine that drains the oil, strains out crumbs and stores it in a sealed container lets you reuse the same batch several times, and it also removes the messiest chore in frying, which is pouring a gallon of hot oil from a heavy pot.

Filtration comes in several forms. Some fryers have an automatic filter and a storage tank built into the base, some have a simple drain valve with a screen, and some include a strainer you fit yourself. This guide ranks the lineup by how well each system works in practice, what it costs in parts to clean and how much oil each pot holds.

products.name: All-Clad 3.5L Electric Deep Fryer With Oil Filtration, 1700W
products.description:
All-Clad's fryer centers on a patented oil filtration system that manages the oil automatically, storing it between uses. A 1700 watt element with adjustable temperature from 300 degrees fries 2.65 pounds of snacks in a 3.5 liter pot, and the listing states the parts are dishwasher safe.

Automatic oil management is the premium feature. After frying, you let the oil cool and run the filter, which strains crumbs and moves the oil into storage inside the machine, ready for the next session. That removes the manual straining, the funnel and the mess. The stainless body is built for years of use.

Against the T-fal 3.5 liter, the All-Clad has a similar capacity and power but a more refined build and dishwasher-safe parts, at a higher price. As with any filtration system, clean the filter and storage after each use, because trapped crumbs spoil oil. A useful routine is to filter the oil the same evening you fry, label the reservoir with the date and note what you cooked, so you remember that the oil that fried fish on Friday should not be used for donuts on Sunday. Many owners keep a small notebook taped inside a cabinet door for exactly this reason. Replace the oil when it darkens, smokes at low temperatures or smells off, and avoid frying strongly flavored foods in oil you plan to reuse.
products.bestFor: Households that fry often and want a premium, low-effort system.
pros: Patented automatic oil filtration and storage
cons: Filter and storage need cleaning after use

products.name: T-fal 3.5L Deep Fryer With Oil Filtration, 1700W
products.description:
T-fal's 3.5 liter model uses an automatic filtration system that filters the oil and stores it in a sealed container, with a 1700 watt element and a thermostat from 300 to 375 degrees. The listing gives 2.65 pounds of food volume.

The sealed storage is practical: oil sits in a closed container instead of an open pot, so it stays cleaner and does not absorb kitchen odors. A thermostat range of 300 to 375 covers most home recipes. It is very close in specs to the All-Clad, and the main difference is the finish, the premium parts and the price tier.

Use the filtration after the oil cools, empty the crumb screen and wipe the container. Replace oil when it darkens, and avoid reusing it after fish or strongly seasoned foods. The T-fal has been a standard for home frying for years, which means replacement baskets and filters are easy to find. That availability matters over a long ownership, because the filter paper or mesh is a wear part, and a fryer whose consumables are hard to buy becomes useless the day the first filter wears out. Check the manual for the replacement schedule and stock a spare.
products.bestFor: Households that want filtration without a premium price.
cons: Less refined finish than the All-Clad

products.name: T-fal EZ Clean 1.8L Compact Deep Fryer With Filtration
products.description:
The EZ Clean packs the same patented automatic filtration into a compact 1.8 liter pot, with a 300 to 375 degree thermostat and a stainless build. The listing gives up to 1.7 pounds of fries per batch and frames it as a small fryer for families.

Compact filtration is a combination few competitors offer. Small households benefit most from reusing oil, because a small pot is emptied and refilled often, yet most filtered fryers are large. The EZ Clean answers that with a body that stores easily and a filter that still handles the oil.

The trade-off is batch size. At 1.7 pounds of fries it feeds two to three people, and a larger meal means frying in rounds. Filter after each use, keep the crumb screen clean and replace the oil on schedule. Compared with the 3.5 liter T-fal, it saves space and oil at the cost of volume. For a couple that fries fish on Friday and wings on Sunday, a small filtered pot is easier to fill and discard than a large one, and the sealed storage keeps oil fresh between those meals. It also fits in a cabinet, which matters in a small kitchen.
products.bestFor: Small households that want filtration in a compact body.
pros: Automatic filtration in a 1.8 liter pot
Fries up to 1.7 lb at a time

products.name: Kalorik Deep Fryer With Oil Filtration

specList.label: Filtration
specList.value: Drains and filters oil for reuse

products.description:
Kalorik's fryer includes an oil filtration system that drains and filters oil for reuse, with adjustable temperature control, a dishwasher-safe basket and an easy-view lid. The maker lists chicken, fries, wings, onion rings, doughnuts and beignets among its targets.

The dishwasher-safe basket shows the focus on cleanup. A fryer basket is one of the messiest parts to wash by hand, and going in a dishwasher saves effort. The filtration lets you save oil, which the listing frames as eco-friendly and economical.

The listing leaves out capacity and wattage details, so check the specification before buying. Use the filtration after the oil cools, empty the crumb screen and wipe the reservoir. Avoid frying battered fish in oil you plan to reuse, since the flavor lingers. Because the listing is thin on numbers, confirm the oil capacity and the wattage on the product page, and look at how large the basket is, since a fryer with a small basket and a big pot is a poor match. If those details are missing, compare against the T-fal's 1700 watts and 3.5 liters as a benchmark.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want filtration and an easy-to-wash basket.

products.name: CATTLEMAN 3L Deep Fryer With Oil Filtration, 1600W
products.description:
CATTLEMAN's deep fryer has a 1600 watt rapid-heating element, a 3 liter pot, a stainless steel body, a 195 to 375 degree temperature range and a 60 minute timer. A filtration solution for messy, debris-filled oil is included, per the product page.

The temperature floor of 195 degrees is the lowest in the guide and allows gentle cooking and warming. The timer adds a layer of control that the T-fal and All-Clad lack. Against those two, the CATTLEMAN has less brand history and a smaller power rating, but more features for the money.

The filtration is described as a set that strains debris, so check how the oil is stored and cleaned before you rely on it. Keep the timer and temperature controls dry, strain after cooling and clean the stainless pot with a non-abrasive pad. It suits cooks who like timers and a wide range. A 60 minute timer is not a safety device, and it should never replace staying nearby while oil is hot, but it helps you hold a consistent cook time for batches of nuggets or wings. The low 195 degree floor also lets you keep fried food warm without overcooking it, which is handy when a big meal comes out in rounds.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a timer and a wide temperature range.
cons: Filtration is less automated than T-fal and All-Clad

products.name: VEVOR 9.51-Qt Electric Deep Fryer, Oil Filtration Upgrade, 1750W
products.description:
VEVOR's single-tank unit holds 9.51 quarts, about 9 liters, of water capacity, runs a 1750 watt heating system with temperature control and includes a faucet-style oil drain valve on the tank. The maker lists an oil filtration upgrade for this version.

The faucet drain is the biggest convenience in the guide. Instead of lifting a pot of hot oil, you place a container under the valve, let the oil cool and open it. That also makes filtering through a strainer easier. At nearly three times the volume of the 3.5 liter models, it suits a restaurant counter, a bar or a family that fries for a crowd.

A large oil volume demands attention: it takes longer to heat, costs more to fill and is heavy to place. Let the oil cool fully before draining, keep the valve closed during frying and check it for leaks. Strain through a fine mesh and filter the oil before storing it. At this volume a drain mishap is a serious burn risk, so place the container before you open the valve, use a container rated for hot liquids and never walk away while it drains. A sturdy stand or counter is essential, since the tank is heavy when full.
products.bestFor: Bars, cafes and large households that need a drain valve.
cons: Large oil volume is costly and slow to heat

buyingCriteria.explanation: The All-Clad, T-fal and T-fal EZ Clean use automatic filters with sealed storage, the Kalorik drains and filters for reuse, the CATTLEMAN includes a filtration set and the VEVOR uses a faucet drain with a filtration upgrade. Automatic systems save effort, while drain valves save lifting. Pick the style that matches how you hate to work. An automatic filter is a closed loop that you never touch with hot oil, so it is the safest for home cooks, while a faucet drain suits a commercial counter where oil volumes make lifting impractical. The simplest systems, a screen and a hand strainer, work too but depend entirely on your discipline.

The T-fal EZ Clean holds 1.8 liters for 1.7 pounds of fries, the 3.5 liter models 2.65 pounds and the VEVOR 9.51 quarts. A bigger pot stabilizes temperature but costs more oil. Choose by the biggest batch you cook regularly. Filtered storage also has a practical limit: a reservoir sized for 3.5 liters of oil will not take 9 liters, so a large pot needs a different approach to storage. Think about where the filtered oil will sit between uses, because a container in a hot kitchen spoils faster than one in a cool pantry.

The All-Clad and T-fal list 1700 watts, the CATTLEMAN 1600 and the VEVOR 1750. Higher wattage recovers faster after food goes in, but oil volume matters too. A 1750 watt element in a 9 liter pot is gentler than the same in a 3.5 liter pot.

A filter adds parts to wash: screens, a reservoir and gaskets. The All-Clad lists dishwasher-safe parts, and the Kalorik lists a dishwasher-safe basket. A system that is hard to clean encourages you to skip it. Before buying, check how many pieces come apart and whether they are dishwasher safe, and consider whether you are willing to wash a screen, a reservoir and a gasket after every session. A well-designed filter takes five minutes to clean, and a badly designed one takes twenty and ends up unused in a cupboard.
The CATTLEMAN covers 195 to 375 degrees, the T-fals 300 to 375. Delicate foods such as donuts like temperatures below 350. A low floor gives more recipes.
Filtration removes crumbs but not flavor or breakdown. Dark, foamy or smoky oil should be replaced no matter how well it is filtered. Fish and spiced foods taint oil for later batches.

faq.q: How does a fryer filter oil?
faq.a: It strains crumbs through a screen and stores the oil in a sealed container. It removes particles but not flavor or breakdown, so oil that has darkened or taken on fish flavor stays that way. Filtering right after the oil cools matters most, because crumbs left in hot oil keep burning and speed its decay.

faq.q: How many times can I reuse oil?
faq.a: A handful of times for plain foods, fewer for breaded or fishy ones. Replace it when it darkens, foams, smokes at a lower temperature than usual or smells rancid. Store filtered oil in a cool, dark place and top it up with fresh oil rather than stretching one batch until it fails.

If you fry often, yes, since oil is the biggest running cost and the messiest chore. Filtration pays back in saved oil and avoided spills. Occasional fryers can strain by hand through a fine mesh and funnel, which costs little and works well enough for a few sessions a year.

faq.q: Can I put the parts in the dishwasher?
faq.a: Only parts listed as dishwasher safe, such as the All-Clad's and Kalorik's basket.

Only with cool oil and a stable container. Check the valve and gasket for leaks before each use, close the valve fully before refilling and never open it while the oil is hot. A drain valve is convenient, but a sloppy habit around it is a burn risk.

No. Let it cool completely first, which can take an hour or more for a full pot. Hot oil can burn you, melt seals and warp plastic parts, and it also flows poorly through filters. Plan the filtering step for after dinner instead of right after the last batch.
